nodes.summary: For every key distribution, permutation family and predicate, if every predictor wins the prediction experiment with probability at most $\tfrac12 + \varepsilon$, then $\varepsilon \ge \tfrac12$: the predictor $y \mapsto b_\alpha(p_\alpha^{-1}(y))$, which inverts the permutation, always wins. In this concrete model, where every function counts as a predictor, the theorems that assume the all-predictor hypothesis…
nodes.title: An unbounded predictor always wins

nodes.summary: The distinguishing advantage between the two worlds of the hard-core experiment: how well a distinguisher tells the hard-core bit from its complement.
nodes.title: Hard-core distinguishing advantage

nodes.summary: Draw a key pair $(\alpha, \tau)$, coins $r$ and a uniform $x \in D$. The distinguisher receives $\alpha$, $p_\alpha(x)$ and the bit $b_\alpha(x)$ (world $0$) or its complement (world $1$), and the experiment outputs its answer.
nodes.title: The hard-core experiment, distinguishing form

nodes.summary: For every distinguisher $A$, its advantage between encryptions of $0$ and $1$ under the scheme equals $2 \lvert \Pr[\text{the predictor built from } A \text{ wins}] with one call. So a distinguisher with advantage $\varepsilon$ gives a predictor of the hard-core bit with advantage $\varepsilon/2$, and an efficient distinguisher an equally efficient predictor: this is the security of encryption from a hard-core…
nodes.title: Goldreich's Proposition 5.3.14, per adversary

nodes.summary: For the scheme, the indistinguishability experiment on the bit $\sigma$ is the hard-core experiment in world $\sigma$: the ciphertext $(p_\alpha(r), \sigma \oplus b(r))$ is the pair $(p_\alpha(r), b(r))$ or $(p_\alpha(r), \lnot b(r))$.
nodes.title: Distinguishing encryptions is distinguishing the hard-core bit

nodes.summary: If every predictor with the predictor's coins wins the prediction experiment with probability at most $\tfrac12 + \varepsilon$, then the scheme has indistinguishable encryptions with error $2\varepsilon$.
nodes.title: All-predictor form of Proposition 5.3.14 (vacuous against unbounded predictors)

nodes.summary: Draw a key pair $(\alpha, \tau)$, coins $r$ and a uniform $x \in D$; the predictor receives $\alpha$ and $p_\alpha(x)$ and wins when its output equals $b_\alpha(x)$. A hard-core predicate is one for which every efficient predictor wins with probability at most $\tfrac12$ plus a negligible amount.
nodes.title: The hard-core prediction experiment

nodes.summary: The distribution of coins of the predictor built from a distinguisher: the distinguisher's coins together with an independent fair bit.
nodes.title: The coins of the predictor

nodes.summary: From a distinguisher $A$: on $\alpha$, $y$ and coins $(r, c)$ with $c$ a bit, run $A$ on $(y, c)$ and output $c$ if $A$ answers $1$, and the complement of $c$ otherwise.
nodes.title: The predictor built from a distinguisher

nodes.summary: If $\mathrm{inv}_\tau(p_\alpha(x)) = x$ for every $x$ and every key pair $(\alpha, \tau)$ in the support of the key distribution, then the scheme is correct: every ciphertext of a bit decrypts to that bit.
nodes.title: Correctness of encryption with a hard-core predicate

nodes.summary: Let key pairs $(\alpha, \tau)$ be drawn from a distribution, let $p_\alpha$ be a permutation of a finite nonempty domain $D$, let $\mathrm{inv}_\tau$ be a function on $D$ (the trapdoor inverse) and let $b_\alpha$ be a predicate on $D$. The public key is $\alpha$ and the secret key is $(\alpha, \tau)$. A bit $\sigma$ is encrypted as $(p_\alpha(r), \sigma \oplus b_\alpha(r))$ for a uniform $r \in D$, and a ciphertext…
nodes.title: Encryption of one bit with a hard-core predicate

nodes.summary: Under the hypothesis of the all-predictor form of Proposition 5.3.14, the scheme is semantically secure with error $2\varepsilon$, for any types of a priori information and of guesses.
nodes.title: All-predictor form of semantic security from a hard-core predicate (vacuous against unbounded predictors)

nodes.summary: Replacing a distinguisher by its negation turns its probability $q$ of outputting $1$ in either world of the hard-core experiment into $1 - q$.
nodes.title: Negating a distinguisher

nodes.summary: Fix the key, the distinguisher's coins and the permutation. With a fair bit $c$ and a uniform $x$, the predictor built from $A$ outputs $b(x)$ with probability $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 \bigl(\Pr_x[A(p(x), b(x)) = 1] - \Pr_x[A(p(x), \lnot b(x)) = 1]\bigr)$. For each $x$ it is right when $c = b(x)$ and $A$ accepts, or when $c \ne b(x)$ and $A$ rejects.
nodes.title: The predictor's success for one key and one coin

nodes.summary: For every distinguisher $A$, the predictor built from $A$, with its coins, wins the prediction experiment with probability the probabilities being those of the hard-core experiment. This exact identity is the step that Goldreich's proof of Proposition 5.3.14 obtains "analogously to the second proof of Theorem 3.4.1" (of his Volume I, not consulted here).
nodes.title: Distinguishing implies predicting
